sources.citation: Shah et al. TN-Eval: Rubric and Evaluation Protocols for Measuring the Quality of Behavioral Therapy Notes. Proc. 63rd ACL (Industry Track), 2025, pp. 178-192.
sources.population: 50 conversations from the high-quality split of AnnoMI (public motivational interviewing demonstrations, English)
sources.raters: 5 internal + 8 note-writing + 9 evaluating licensed US therapists; rubric validated with 17 external therapists
sources.unit: rubric item per SOAP section; sentence for conciseness; sentence for faithfulness
sources.format: binary item coverage, sentence labels, 3-way hallucination label; 5-point Likert baseline for comparison
sources.analysis: Krippendorff's alpha, raw agreement, correlation of automatic with human scores
sources.key_results: TNH-Eval rubric alpha 0.49-0.62 vs Likert alpha 0.08-0.18. Likert ranks LLM notes above human notes on every dimension; the rubric reverses that for faithfulness.
sources.limitations: Public MI demonstrations are not routine clinical sessions. English only. Note sources were revealed to annotators. No Czech evidence.

sources.citation: Croxford et al. Development and validation of the provider documentation summarization quality instrument for large language models. J Am Med Inform Assoc, 2025. doi:10.1093/jamia/ocaf068. PMID 40323321.
sources.population: 779 multi-document EHR summaries, multiple specialties, real-world data; psychiatry and psychotherapy notes explicitly excluded
sources.analysis: Cronbach's alpha, ICC, Krippendorff's alpha, factor analysis, semi-Delphi, high vs low quality discrimination
sources.key_results: Cronbach's alpha 0.879 (95% CI 0.867-0.891); ICC 0.867 (95% CI 0.867-0.868); 4-factor model explaining 58% of variance (organization, clarity, accuracy, utility).
sources.limitations: Psychotherapy notes were excluded from the validation corpus by design, so transfer to psychotherapy documentation is untested. Substantive validity rests on weak length correlations (beta about -0.2).

sources.citation: Adhikary et al. Clinically Grounded AI-Scribing in Psychotherapy: Benchmarking LLMs Against Expert Documentation in the iCARE Framework. medRxiv 2025.06.25.25330252.
sources.population: iHOPE, derived from the HOPE dataset of pre-recorded counselling videos published on YouTube, re-transcribed and diarised with WhisperX
sources.raters: clinical experts; annotation validated in multiple stages
sources.analysis: benchmarking of 11 LLMs with automatic metrics and expert assessment
sources.key_results: 17 aspects covering identifiers, history, crisis markers, mental state, therapy type and technique, therapist reflections, action plan and next session.
sources.limitations: Preprint. Public counselling videos, not routine care. Aspect 1 requires patient name and contact details, which conflicts with data minimisation. The MSE aspect asks only for positive findings.

sources.citation: Stetson et al. Assessing Electronic Note Quality Using the Physician Documentation Quality Instrument (PDQI-9). Appl Clin Inform 2012;3(2):164-174. doi:10.4338/aci-2011-11-ra-0070. PMC3347480, PMID 22577483.
sources.population: inpatient electronic notes, US academic centre
sources.key_results: The 9-item instrument condensed from a longer preliminary version.
sources.limitations: General medicine, not psychotherapy. The preliminary-development report of the same study family was not retrieved in this round.

sources.citation: Stetson et al. Preliminary development of the physician documentation quality instrument. J Am Med Inform Assoc 2008;15(4):534-541. doi:10.1197/jamia.M2404. PMID 18436914.
sources.limitations: Full text not open access and not obtained. Linked to S4 as the earlier report of the same instrument family; the two are not independent confirmations.

sources.citation: Walker KJ, Wang A, Dunlop W, Rodda H, et al. The 9-Item Physician Documentation Quality Instrument (PDQI-9) score is not useful in evaluating EMR (scribe) note quality in Emergency Medicine. Appl Clin Inform 2017;8(3):981-993. doi:10.4338/ACI2017050080. PMID 28956888.
sources.population: 110 scribed and 110 non-scribed emergency department notes, Cabrini ED, Australia
sources.raters: 2 per note: an emergency physician plus a senior resident or senior nurse; raters were NOT trained and no pre-study agreement on standards was established
sources.format: PDQI-9 5-point Likert, plus two yes/no items
sources.analysis: Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation between raters, ANOVA of rater effects, discrimination of good from poor notes
sources.key_results: Cronbach's alpha 0.93 but between-rater Pearson r = 0.07 (p = 0.270); rater main effect F(25,206) = 1.93, p = 0.007; unable to distinguish good from poor notes, F(3,34) = 1.15, p = 0.342.
sources.limitations: One department, one country, emergency medicine. Its value here is the negative result and the untrained-rater condition, not generalisation to psychotherapy.

sources.citation: Adhikary et al. Exploring the Efficacy of Large Language Models in Summarizing Mental Health Counseling Sessions: Benchmark Study. JMIR Ment Health 2024;11:e57306. doi:10.2196/57306. PMID 39042893.
sources.population: 191 counselling sessions, 11 543 utterances, from publicly accessible video platforms (MEMO dataset)
sources.format: three counselling components; expert rating on six acceptability parameters
sources.analysis: ROUGE-1/2/L and BERTScore plus qualitative expert assessment
sources.key_results: Task-specific LLMs win on automatic metrics, yet 'expert assessments indicate that these models are not yet reliable for clinical application'. Experts rated on affective attitude, burden, ethicality, coherence, opportunity costs and perceived effectiveness.
sources.limitations: Public videos, English. The three components are a task definition, not a validated quality model.

sources.citation: Scialom et al. QuestEval: Summarization Asks for Fact-based Evaluation. EMNLP 2021, pp. 6594-6604.
sources.format: QA-based precision and recall without a reference summary
sources.key_results: A question-answering formulation of factual consistency and relevance that needs no reference summary.
sources.limitations: General-domain news text. No clinical or Czech validation. Retrieval of an answer is not proof that the answer is clinically correct.

sources.citation: Fabbri et al. QAFactEval: Improved QA-Based Factual Consistency Evaluation for Summarization. NAACL 2022, pp. 2587-2601.
sources.key_results: Component-level analysis of QA-based consistency metrics; improved answerability handling.
sources.limitations: General domain. Unanswerable questions are a distinct outcome from wrong answers, and conflating them distorts the score.

sources.citation: Min et al. FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation. EMNLP 2023, pp. 12076-12100.
sources.format: supported / not supported per atomic fact, against a knowledge source
sources.key_results: Decomposition into atomic facts makes factual precision measurable at a granularity that whole-text ratings cannot reach.
sources.limitations: Precision only; it does not measure omission. Atomicity of decomposition is itself an unvalidated step. No clinical or Czech validation.

sources.citation: Terwee et al. COSMIN methodology for evaluating the content validity of patient-reported outcome measures: a Delphi study. Qual Life Res 2018;27:1159-1170. doi:10.1007/s11136-018-1829-0.
sources.key_results: Relevance, comprehensiveness and comprehensibility are the three content validity components, judged against a stated target population and purpose.
sources.limitations: Designed for patient-reported outcome scales. A documentation checklist rated by a third party is not a PROM, so the criteria need explicit adaptation.

sources.citation: Boateng et al. Best Practices for Developing and Validating Scales for Health, Social, and Behavioral Research: A Primer. Front Public Health 2018;6:149. doi:10.3389/fpubh.2018.00149.
sources.key_results: Item generation, content validity, pre-testing, then dimensionality, reliability and validity testing, in that order.
sources.limitations: Assumes a reflective latent construct. A heterogeneous error checklist is not automatically such a scale and should not be forced into one.

sources.citation: American Psychological Association. Record Keeping Guidelines. Am Psychol 2007;62(9):993-1004. doi:10.1037/0003-066X.62.9.993.
sources.format: 13 numbered guidelines with rationale and application
sources.key_results: Guideline 8 asks the psychologist to be attentive to the situational context in which records are created and how it influences their content.
sources.limitations: EXPIRED BY ITS OWN TERMS. The document states it was 'scheduled to expire 10 years from February 16, 2007'. Whether a successor is in force was not established in this round. US jurisdiction; it is not a Czech requirement.

sources.citation: Decree No. 444/2024 Coll., on medical documentation (Vyhlaska c. 444/2024 Sb., o zdravotnicke dokumentaci). Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic, adopted 2024-12-19, in force from 2025-01-01.
sources.population: all health services provided in the Czech Republic
sources.key_results: Section 2 enumerates the required content of medical documentation, including provider and patient identification, the author of each entry, and information on the course and outcome of the services provided.
sources.limitations: It replaced Decree No. 98/2012 Coll., which was repealed with effect from 2025-01-01. It states required elements, not quality. Presence of a required field is not evidence that its content is correct.

sources.citation: Peters MDJ et al. Updated methodological guidance for the conduct of scoping reviews. JBI Evid Synth 2020;18(10):2119-2126. doi:10.11124/JBIES-20-00167.
sources.key_results: Study selection 'is usually conducted by a minimum of two reviewers' and data extraction 'should involve at least two reviewers'.
sources.limitations: This round has one investigator and an AI assistant, which is a declared deviation from that guidance.

sources.citation: Tricco AC et al. PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR): Checklist and Explanation. Ann Intern Med 2018;169(7):467-473. doi:10.7326/M18-0850.
sources.key_results: A 20-item checklist for reporting scoping reviews.
sources.limitations: The retrieved copy is the accepted manuscript from a repository, not the version of record; its Supplement 2 item elaboration was not obtained.

sources.citation: Rethlefsen ML et al. PRISMA-S: an extension to the PRISMA Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews. Syst Rev 2021;10:39. doi:10.1186/s13643-020-01542-z.
sources.key_results: Item 8 requires search strategies 'copied and pasted exactly as run'; item 13 the date of the last search; item 15 total records per source.
sources.limitations: Reporting guidance only; following it does not make a search comprehensive.

sources.citation: Keren L, Klein A, Bar-Shachar Y, Liakata M, Atzil-Slonim D et al. Clinical Summaries of Social Media Timelines for Mental Health Monitoring: Human Versus Large Language Model. JMIR Form Res 2026. PMID 41894679, PMC13069367.
sources.population: 33 human-written expert summaries over social media timelines (TalkLife), sampled from a 500-timeline dataset
sources.raters: 3 clinical psychology graduate students, trained in 2 sessions with guideline refinement under an expert clinical supervisor; blind peer rating
sources.format: five 1-5 Likert metrics: factual consistency, meaning preservation / general usefulness, and aspect-specific usefulness for three core clinical aspects
sources.analysis: Likert comparisons plus automatic linguistic-diversity analysis
sources.key_results: Three evaluation dimensions: salient meaning preservation, factual consistency and personalisation. Evaluators observed a trade-off: model summaries were more comprehensive, human summaries better at focusing on the clinically salient. Human summaries showed significantly greater linguistic diversity.
sources.limitations: Social media timelines, not therapy sessions. Raters rated their own peers' work. The diversity proxy varied with the embedding model chosen, which the authors report as an inconsistency.

sources.citation: Keren L, Klein A, Bar-Shachar Y, Liakata M, Atzil-Slonim D. A comparative evaluation of LLM-generated and clinician-written psychotherapy session summaries. Psychother Res 2026. doi:10.1080/10503307.2026.2729093. PMID 42715612.
sources.population: 1008 segment-level summaries (504 clinician-written, 504 LLaMA-3.1-70B) over 108 five-minute segments from 36 sessions of 16-session supportive-expressive psychodynamic therapy for depression, 58 patients with MDD, 13 therapists, Bar-Ilan community clinic. Hebrew transcripts machine-translated to English; speech-turns randomised before translation and reordered locally afterwards for confidentiality.
sources.raters: summaries by 4 clinical psychology graduate trainees after intensive calibration; evaluation by 3 independent undergraduate judges after group seminars plus 15 practical meetings of 1.5 h and a jointly scored 10-segment training set, with weekly drift checks
sources.unit: one MIND component of one five-minute segment
sources.format: three 1-5 criteria: factual consistency, salient meaning preservation, clinical value; clinical value not applied to Main Topics Discussed
sources.analysis: paired permutation tests, 10 000 iterations, Cohen's d; annotation reliability by Gwet's AC1/AC2 and Jaccard, chosen over kappa for prevalence robustness
sources.key_results: Judge reliability ICC .81 factual consistency, .71 salient meaning, .65 clinical value. Clinicians higher on all three: d = 1.54, 0.70 and 0.51. The single reversal is salient meaning on Main Topics Discussed, d = -0.46. No difference on clinical value for Dyadic Relationship (p = .696) or Micro-Level Outcome (p = .070). Error types differ by component: hallucination on the surface task, misinterpretation and misattributed interventions on the clinical ones. Clinical value scored lowest for humans too (3.94).
sources.limitations: Summaries written by trainees, not experienced therapists. Segments, not whole sessions, with context limited to the current session. Full transcripts were found to dilute the model and were deliberately replaced by a distilled preamble. Blinding success was never behaviourally tested. Length, terminology and structure were deliberately aligned between sources, which is why this study cannot be read as evidence that models cover more.

families.label: Fidelity to the source and the status of information
families.summary: Whether a statement in the note matches what was said in the session, and whether its origin, time, certainty and speaker are preserved.
families.boundary: Boundary with F3: an unsupported interpretation is a fidelity failure, but a justified interpretation grounded in the source belongs to synthesis. One wrong statement can be found by QA and by claim verification; those are not two independent errors.

families.label: Coverage of essential content
families.summary: Whether the note carries what is genuinely essential for the given recipient and purpose, not whether it filled every field.
families.boundary: Boundary with F6: a field required by a specification is a specification criterion, not evidence that the content is clinically essential. Omission and an explicit negative finding must not be conflated.

families.label: Processing and clinical synthesis
families.summary: Whether the note builds relations between pieces of information justifiably and to the degree the purpose requires, without being rewarded for inventing a clinical story.
families.boundary: Overlaps with F1: every synthesis is also a statement whose support can be verified. Kept separate because missing synthesis is not the same as false synthesis.

families.label: Comprehensibility, organisation and economy
families.summary: Whether the note can be read and navigated, and whether every part of it serves something.
families.boundary: The shortest note is not the best one. Sentence relevance, redundancy, level of detail and bare length must be kept distinguishable; PDSQI measures them with one attribute, TN-Eval in another way.

families.label: Respect, privacy and safety of sharing
families.summary: Whether the note speaks about a person in a way that holds up when they read it, and whether it carries sensitive detail its purpose does not need.
families.boundary: The requirements here depend most on jurisdiction and recipient and are least supported by direct research on psychotherapy notes. iCARE asks for contact details; that contradicts data minimisation rather than confirming it.

families.label: Traceability and conformance to the specification
families.summary: Whether a statement can be traced to the source and whether the note meets a stated, declared specification.
families.boundary: Validity of a citation, its semantic support and the coverage of claims by citations are three different things. Meeting a decree is not evidence of quality, and the reverse.

families.label: Usability in the task
families.summary: Whether the note actually carries the task it was written for: taking over care, supervising, understanding as a client, passing an audit.
families.boundary: These are outcome indicators, not properties of the text. They are measured on people doing the task; a number from an LLM is a stand-in here, not evidence.

conditions.label: Raters must be trained on the instrument
conditions.detail: PDSQI-9 with trained raters: ICC 0.867. The same instrument lineage (PDQI-9) with untrained raters and no prior agreement on standards: Pearson r = 0.07 (p = 0.270) and an inability to tell a good note from a poor one, F(3,34) = 1.15, p = 0.342. Different instrument versions, samples, rater pools and statistics, so the pair motivates training without establishing its causal effect or size (audit A06); training is advisable before any use, and its effect is to be measured, not assumed.

conditions.label: Internal consistency is not rater agreement
conditions.detail: In the same study, Cronbach's alpha = 0.93 and at the same time r = 0.07 between raters. A high alpha says nothing about whether two people agree on the same note.

conditions.label: Task decomposition and response format must not change at once
conditions.detail: TN-Eval shows higher agreement for the rubric than for Likert scales and, for faithfulness, even a reversed ranking of systems. The rubric, however, changes the unit, the instruction and the response format at the same time, so the difference cannot be attributed to the scale alone.

conditions.label: Automatic metrics and expert judgement diverge
conditions.detail: MentalCLOUDS: models lead on ROUGE and BERTScore, and yet the experts conclude that they are not reliable for clinical use. The divergence is a result, not a measurement error.

conditions.label: A judge can handle coverage, not faithfulness
conditions.detail: TN-Eval: LLM-as-a-judge is usable for completeness but correlates poorly for conciseness and faithfulness; their automatic faithfulness therefore uses AlignScore, not a judge.

candidates.label: Support of claims in the source
candidates.definition: Every factual claim in the note has support in the session transcript or in another declared source. Lack of support divides into invented (the source has nothing of the kind) and distorted (the source says something else).
candidates.origin_note: Existed in the project as Factual agreement, from the reproduction of the instrument. The review now adds the verbatim three-way typology from TN-Eval and the fabrication/falsification distinction from PDSQI-9. Finding a source does not change where the idea came from.

evidence.quote: categorizing hallucinations into (1) Out-of-nowhere, (2) Misinterpreted Information, or (3) No Error
evidence.supports: A three-way typology of fidelity error, rated per sentence against the transcript.
evidence.our_adaptation: TN-Eval annotates with licensed therapists in English; automation and Czech are our step.

evidence.quote: the vulnerability of the attribute Accurate to hallucinations and the attribute Thorough to omissions
evidence.supports: Separation of inaccuracy from omission as two different vulnerabilities.
evidence.our_adaptation: PDSQI rates the whole summary with one Likert item; the claim as unit is our proposal.

candidates.inputs: session transcript, note, segmentation into claims
candidates.applicability: Always. Unavailable context or a failed retrieval makes a claim unassessable; that is not the same as false.

examples.positive: Transcript: the client says they sleep about four hours. Note: The client reports sleeping about four hours.
examples.negative: Note: The client reports insomnia since the divorce. No divorce was mentioned in the session.
examples.boundary: Note: The client seemed tired. The transcript only contains a yawn; a therapist's observation can be neither verified nor refuted from a text transcript.

candidates.measurement: Verification of claims against the source with four outcomes: supported, contradicted, unsupported, unassessable.
candidates.error_consequence: An invented fact propagates into further care and the client reads it as something said about them.
candidates.validation: Direct evidence from S1 for English and public MI demonstrations. No Czech validation.
candidates.overlaps: K02-K04; one wrong claim is one finding, not four.

candidates.label: Preservation of the originator of a statement
candidates.definition: The note preserves who said or observed what: the client's statement, the therapist's observation, a third party's information, information from earlier documentation.
candidates.origin_note: Follows from the SOAP section definitions in TN-Eval, which separate subjective statements from observations.

evidence.quote: Avoid including any subjective statements or self-reported information from the client.
evidence.supports: Separating the originator is an explicit requirement of the format, not our improvement.
evidence.our_adaptation: TN-Eval handles it by placement in a section; measuring attribution inside a sentence is our proposal.

candidates.applicability: Requires a transcript with speaker roles. Without diarisation it cannot be measured.

examples.positive: The client reports that his partner reproaches him for drinking.
examples.negative: The partner reproaches the client for drinking. The client's belief has become a fact about a third person.
examples.boundary: The client agreed to try... An agreement has two originators; attributing it to one is misleading.

candidates.measurement: Part of claim comparison: agreement on the actor is a condition of the verdict supported.
candidates.error_consequence: A belief recorded as a fact about a third person is both a fidelity error and an intrusion on the rights of someone who is not the client and has no access to the note.
candidates.validation: Indirect; no study found measured attribution separately.

candidates.label: Time and change of state
candidates.definition: The note preserves when what happened and what is current as opposed to past: current state, history, intention, plan.
candidates.origin_note: Existed locally. The review adds a cautionary support: in PDSQI-9 the Up-to-Date attribute from PDQI-9 was removed as redundant.

evidence.quote: Two PDQI-9 attributes, Up-to-Date and Consistent, were removed
evidence.supports: Temporality was a separate attribute in PDQI-9 and the PDSQI-9 authors judged it redundant.
evidence.our_adaptation: We take this as a warning against a separate temporal column; we propose to measure time as part of claim agreement.

candidates.applicability: Longitudinal tasks require previous notes; those must not be slipped to a task that is not supposed to have them.

examples.positive: In the last session he refused; today he is considering it.
examples.negative: The client takes antidepressants. The session was about use two years ago.
examples.boundary: Plans to contact his brother. An intention voiced in the session, not an event that took place.

candidates.measurement: Agreement on time is a condition of the verdict supported. A separate temporal score is not introduced before it is shown to add information over K01.
candidates.error_consequence: A past state presented as current changes the clinical decision.
candidates.validation: PDSQI-9's own experience rather argues against a separate scale.

candidates.label: Certainty, hypothesis and agreement
candidates.definition: The note preserves epistemic status: what is certain, what is the therapist's hypothesis, what is a suggestion and what is an agreement between therapist and client.
candidates.origin_note: A local refinement. The review gives it support in that TN-Eval expects hypotheses in the Assessment section as hypotheses.

evidence.quote: Summarize the clinical impressions and hypotheses regarding the client's issues.
evidence.supports: A hypothesis is the expected content of the section, so it should remain a hypothesis.
evidence.our_adaptation: TN-Eval does not measure whether the note keeps the status of a hypothesis; that is our proposal.

candidates.applicability: Always.

examples.positive: I am considering whether this is avoidant behaviour; to be checked in the next session.
examples.negative: This is avoidant behaviour. A consideration has become a conclusion.
examples.boundary: We agreed on a sleep diary. If the suggestion was made and the client stayed silent, it is not an agreement.

candidates.measurement: Agreement on modality is a condition of the verdict supported; it is also tracked as a separate error type.
candidates.error_consequence: A suggestion elevated to an agreement creates in further care a commitment the client never signed up to.
candidates.validation: None direct.

candidates.label: Coverage of essential content weighted by importance
candidates.definition: The share of essential information from the session that the note carries, where essentiality is graded and derived from the source and the purpose, not from the existence of a field in a form.
candidates.origin_note: The strongest change against the previous map. TN-Eval grades importance into five levels; our reproduction treats the items as an equal-weighted checklist.

evidence.quote: Mandatory, Mandatory in certain circumstances, Highly recommended, Good to have, and Optional.
evidence.supports: Five-level importance of items, verified with five therapists at Fleiss' kappa 0.68 and Krippendorff's alpha 0.73.
evidence.our_adaptation: Carrying the grading into the score and adding purpose dependence is our step.

evidence.quote: The full note score is computed as a micro average, weighted by section rubric elements.
evidence.supports: Even coverage itself is not a plain share over all items.

evidence.quote: are only considered when classified as pertinent or potentially pertinent
evidence.supports: An omission counts only when it is relevant to the use and the recipient.

candidates.mode: yes/no per unit, then a share per importance level
candidates.unit: information unit derived from the source, with an assigned importance level
candidates.inputs: transcript, an information bank built before seeing the note, note
candidates.applicability: Information that was not said in the session must not be counted as omitted. The bank must exist before exposure to the candidate note.

examples.positive: Self-harm was mentioned and the note carries it; an item of the Mandatory level.
examples.negative: Self-harm was mentioned and the note lacks it. One Mandatory omission weighs more than three Good-to-have omissions.
examples.boundary: The session contains nothing about medication. The item is not applicable, not unmet, and does not belong in the denominator.

candidates.measurement: QA against a bank built from the source, with the score reported separately for each importance level. Never one average number.
candidates.error_consequence: Omitting risk information is a different class of error from omitting a homework task; blending them into one percentage erases the difference.
candidates.validation: The grading is supported in S1 with the stated agreement. Transfer to Czech unverified.

candidates.label: Acknowledged information gap
candidates.definition: The note distinguishes three things: that something was not said, that it was said to be absent, and that nobody asked about it.
candidates.origin_note: Arose from a repeated finding in the reviews of this project, where a model wrote Nil and received a full score. The review adds a concrete counterexample in iCARE.

evidence.quote: an assessment of the most recent mental state
evidence.supports: iCARE asks for the MSE as a structured field.
evidence.our_adaptation: The conclusion that the MSE cannot be filled from a text transcript without observational data, and that an empty field is not a normal finding, is our adaptation, not a claim of iCARE.

candidates.applicability: Always, but the meaning differs by topic: an unmentioned risk is not an excluded risk.

examples.positive: Asked about suicidal thoughts, denies.
examples.negative: Suicidal thoughts: none. Nobody asked about them in the session.
examples.boundary: No risks. A summary that cannot be assigned to any question from the session.

candidates.measurement: A three-way outcome per information unit: present, explicitly negated in the source, absent from the source. Absence is never converted to zero nor dropped from the denominator.
candidates.error_consequence: A note that manufactures a negative finding gives further care false reassurance.
candidates.validation: No direct study; the support is project experience and the contrast with iCARE.

candidates.label: Relevance for a specific recipient
candidates.definition: What is essential changes with who reads the note and why. The same information can be necessary for taking over care and superfluous in a client summary.
candidates.origin_note: Existed as Relevance for the recipient. The review adds that PDSQI ties relevance to the use case and the intended provider.

evidence.quote: A pertinent omission refers to details relevant to a patient's expected
evidence.supports: Relevance is defined against the expected use, not absolutely.
evidence.our_adaptation: Our four purposes are our construction, not PDSQI's.

evidence.quote: relevance
evidence.supports: Relevance is judged against a declared target population and purpose.
evidence.our_adaptation: COSMIN aims at PROMs; a documentation criterion rated by a third party is not a PROM.

candidates.inputs: information bank with purpose labels, note, declared purpose
candidates.applicability: Requires a purpose declared in advance. Otherwise relevance is unmeasurable.

examples.positive: A detail about medication is essential for continuity and optional in a client summary.
examples.negative: One relevance score across all four purposes.
examples.boundary: Risk information: the one topic where essentiality does not diverge across purposes.

candidates.measurement: Coverage is reported separately for each purpose and never summed.
candidates.error_consequence: A universal score rewards a note that is good for one recipient and unusable for another.
candidates.validation: Indirect. Our four purposes are not a validated taxonomy.

candidates.label: Risk and safety
candidates.definition: A content topic: suicidality, self-harm, danger to others, abuse, crisis markers. It is not a quality construct; it is the topic with the highest error severity.
candidates.origin_note: In TN-Eval safety is the only Mandatory-level item among the general items; in iCARE it has a separate aspect, Crisis Markers.

evidence.quote: Clearly reflect that the practitioner assessed for and addressed any safety concerns
evidence.supports: Safety is mandatory across sections, not the content of one of them.

evidence.quote: indicators that suggest that the patient may be at risk of harming themselves or others
evidence.supports: A separate structured field for crisis markers.

candidates.applicability: The topic occurs rarely; rarity is not a reason to drop the item.

examples.positive: A mention of hopelessness is marked as risk-related in the bank and the note carries it.
examples.negative: The mention of hopelessness is missing, and yet overall coverage comes out at 85%.
examples.boundary: The client speaks about the end ambiguously. The item is disputed, not automatically risk-related.

candidates.measurement: Reported as a separate, undilutable layer above coverage and fidelity. A negative claim about risk findings requires complete assessment of the declared scope.
candidates.error_consequence: The highest. A single omission can be clinically decisive.
candidates.validation: Content support in S1 and S3. No study found measures risk detection in a generated note against a human standard.

candidates.label: Justification of created relations
candidates.definition: If the note connects pieces of information into a relation, a link or a conclusion, that relation is grounded in the source and appropriate to the purpose.
candidates.origin_note: A local refinement derived from the PDSQI attribute Synthesized. The review confirms that PDSQI rewards synthesis, and at the same time shows why that is a risk for us.

evidence.quote: Abstraction, Reasoning, Consistency
evidence.supports: Synthesis is a separate attribute in PDSQI-9, linked to abstraction and reasoning.
evidence.our_adaptation: PDSQI-9 was validated on EHR summaries, where clinical integration is the goal. In a note meant for the client the same integration may be inappropriate; that is our conclusion.

evidence.quote: defines the type of psychotherapy used in the treatment
evidence.supports: iCARE expects the type of therapy to be named.
evidence.our_adaptation: Our conclusion that a generally supportive conversation should not automatically become a named intervention is an adaptation.

candidates.mode: yes/no for support plus ordinal appropriateness
candidates.applicability: The purpose decides how much synthesis is wanted. The mere amount of clinical reasoning cannot be rewarded.

examples.positive: The client himself links avoiding meetings to a fear of being judged by others.
examples.negative: The note concludes social phobia although no such link was made in the session.
examples.boundary: The note calls the conversation cognitive restructuring when the therapist was only exploring how the client thinks.

candidates.measurement: Verification of the relation against the source plus a judgement of appropriateness to the purpose; two separate statements.
candidates.error_consequence: An invented clinical link looks like an expert conclusion and travels on.
candidates.validation: PDSQI-9 has validation for the Synthesized attribute on a different population that explicitly excluded psychotherapy.

candidates.label: Follow-through and next steps
candidates.definition: The note carries what is needed to continue: the plan, agreed tasks, open questions, the date.
candidates.origin_note: TN-Eval and iCARE both have separate mandatory items for the plan.

evidence.quote: Future Interventions: Planned therapeutic techniques or strategies to be used in future sessions. Importance: Mandatory
evidence.supports: Future interventions and the follow-up meeting are items of the Mandatory level.

evidence.location: aspects 16-17 Action Plan, Next Session Details
evidence.quote: a structured plan for ongoing treatment and goals for the patient
evidence.supports: The plan and the details of the next session are separate aspects.

candidates.unit: information unit of the plan type
candidates.applicability: A session without an agreed plan must not be penalised for a missing plan.

examples.positive: A sleep diary agreed until the next session in a week.
examples.negative: The note states a date that was not mentioned in the session.
examples.boundary: The therapist hinted at a plan but did not agree it. A note that presents it as agreed errs in modality, not in content.

candidates.measurement: Coverage of plan-type items, separately from the other content.
candidates.error_consequence: A missing plan breaks continuity; an invented plan creates a false commitment.
candidates.validation: Content support in S1 and S3.

candidates.label: Economy: every sentence serves something
candidates.definition: The share of sentences that carry essential content. Measured by the relation of a sentence to content, not by the length of the text.
candidates.origin_note: Directly from TN-Eval, where conciseness is defined by the relation of a sentence to a rubric item.

evidence.quote: This metric measures whether each sentence contributes to a rubric item.
evidence.supports: Economy is the share of needed sentences, not length.

evidence.quote: correlations between note length and scores for Succinct
evidence.supports: In PDSQI-9 a longer summary is rated as less succinct, beta about -0.2.
evidence.our_adaptation: We take this as a weak relation, not as proof that shorter is better.

candidates.mode: yes/no per sentence, then a share
candidates.applicability: An empty or very short note must not receive high economy without its coverage being reported at the same time.

examples.positive: Four of five sentences carry essential content.
examples.negative: A one-sentence note has economy 1.00 and coverage 0.08; only both may be reported.
examples.boundary: A sentence that carries no content but holds the text together; dropping it is a debatable decision, not an error.

candidates.measurement: The share of sentences tied to at least one information unit; always reported beside coverage, never alone.
candidates.error_consequence: Economy reported on its own rewards an empty note.
candidates.validation: Direct evidence from S1; in S1, however, automatic economy is the dimension where the judge correlates worst with humans.

candidates.label: Organisation and orientation in the text
candidates.definition: The note is structured so that the reader finds what they look for, and content is in its expected place.
candidates.origin_note: The PDSQI attribute Organized; TN-Eval additionally measures whether content belongs to its section.

evidence.quote: well-formed and structured in a way that helps the reader understand the patient's clinical course
evidence.supports: Organisation is defined by its service to the reader.

evidence.quote: We observe perfect IAA among 5 experts for the appropriate section for each key characteristic
evidence.supports: Five experts agreed perfectly, during rubric design, on which section a rubric item belongs to. Placement is therefore well defined; the reliability of rating it on actual notes is not established by that.
evidence.our_adaptation: Using placement as a separate measure is our proposal.

candidates.mode: yes/no per unit times section, then a share
candidates.unit: information unit times section; the whole note for overall organisation
candidates.applicability: Only for tasks that prescribe a structure.

examples.positive: The therapist's observation is in the Objective section.
examples.negative: The therapist's interpretation appears in the Subjective section as a client statement.
examples.boundary: A client quotation inside Assessment: the content belongs elsewhere, but it serves to document the conclusion.

candidates.measurement: The share of information units in their expected place. Separately from whether they are present at all.
candidates.error_consequence: Correct content in the wrong place changes its originator and the reader reads it differently.
candidates.validation: The agreement of five experts on placing items into sections is documented in S1 during rubric design; rating the placement of content in actual notes is not validated.

candidates.label: Comprehensibility for the given reader
candidates.definition: The note is linguistically comprehensible to the person it is meant for. For a client that means a different language than for a colleague.
candidates.origin_note: Locally from PDSQI Comprehensible. The review shows it is a separate factor.

evidence.quote: 4-factor model explaining 58% of the variance, representing organization, clarity, accuracy, and utility
evidence.supports: Clarity separates empirically from organisation, accuracy and utility.
evidence.our_adaptation: The factor structure comes from physicians rating EHR summaries. It cannot be transferred to psychotherapy notes or to reading by a client without verification.

candidates.applicability: Measurable only against a specific recipient.

examples.positive: The client version uses no unexplained technical terms.
examples.negative: The client version contains abbreviations without explanation.
examples.boundary: A technical term the client used in the session themselves.

candidates.measurement: Judgement against the declared recipient; automatic readability indices are a stand-in, not evidence of understanding.
candidates.error_consequence: An incomprehensible client summary fails its only purpose.
candidates.validation: Factor support from S2 on a different population. No Czech readability verification.

candidates.label: Non-stigmatising language
candidates.definition: The note does not use language that belittles the client, questions their credibility or reduces them to a diagnosis or a behaviour.
candidates.origin_note: PDSQI added Stigmatizing as one of two entirely new attributes because of the behaviour of language models.

evidence.quote: Two new attributes were added to address concerns in LLM-generated summaries: use of stigmatizing
evidence.supports: Stigmatising language is a separate attribute in PDSQI-9, introduced precisely because of the models.
evidence.our_adaptation: PDSQI gives example words in English; converting that into a Czech list of forbidden words is an inadmissible simplification and is supported by no source.

evidence.quote: Never describe other clients and staff in a derogatory manner.
evidence.supports: Professionalism includes the way other persons are spoken about.

candidates.mode: marking of a span plus type (quotation / author)
candidates.inputs: note; the source too, for judging context
candidates.applicability: A quotation of the client's own words is judged differently from the note author's wording.

examples.positive: The client did not come to three sessions in recent weeks.
examples.negative: The client is uncooperative and manipulative.
examples.boundary: The client says of himself that he is lazy; a verbatim quotation is not the same as the author's judgement.

candidates.measurement: Marking of spans with an indication of whether it is a quotation or the author's wording. Not a dictionary filter.
candidates.error_consequence: The client reads a condemnation of themselves. It damages the therapeutic relationship and it is a permanent record.
candidates.validation: The existence of the attribute in S2 is documented; its Czech form is not verified at all.

candidates.label: Necessity of sensitive detail
candidates.definition: The note contains only the sensitive detail its declared purpose needs; the rest is generalised or left out.
candidates.origin_note: A proposal of the investigator from earlier deliberations of the project. The review did NOT confirm it; it found the opposite requirement instead. That is the reason to keep it as an explicitly unsupported proposal.

evidence.quote: socio-demographic details such as name, age, sex, contact information
evidence.supports: DOES NOT SUPPORT minimisation. iCARE asks, on the contrary, for the name and contact details.
evidence.our_adaptation: The tension between this requirement and data minimisation is a finding, not support.

evidence.quote: Psychotherapy notes were excluded due to their highly sensitive nature and additional regulatory protections
evidence.supports: The sensitivity of psychotherapy notes is acknowledged so far as to exclude them from the validation study.
evidence.our_adaptation: That is evidence of sensitivity, not of how to measure it in a note.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] the patient's identification and contact details
evidence.supports: The Czech decree requires identification and contact details, the opposite of minimisation.
evidence.our_adaptation: Minimisation therefore cannot concern the fields the law requires; it can concern free text.

candidates.applicability: Must not delete clinically decisive content. A conflict with a legal requirement is resolved in favour of the law and recorded.

examples.positive: The client summary mentions a family conflict without identifying the third person by name.
examples.negative: The note for supervision gives the full name and employer of the client's partner.
examples.boundary: A detail about a third person that is necessary for assessing risk.

candidates.measurement: Human judgement only for now. We propose to postpone automatic measurement.
candidates.error_consequence: Superfluous sensitive detail harms the client and third persons and cannot be taken back.
candidates.validation: NONE. This is the least supported candidate in the registry and is marked as such.

candidates.label: Context of the record's creation
candidates.definition: The note carries information about the circumstances in which it was created, because those affect how its content is to be read.
candidates.origin_note: Corresponds to Guideline 8 of the APA Record Keeping Guidelines. The source, however, is past its own expiry date.

evidence.location: Guideline 8, Preserving the Context of Records
evidence.quote: attentive to the situational context in which records are created and how that context may influence the content of those records
evidence.supports: The context of creation is a professional requirement for record keeping.
evidence.our_adaptation: The APA guidelines themselves state an expiry ten years from 2007-02-16. We use them as a historical, not a current, requirement, and a US standard is not a Czech requirement.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] the given name or names and the surname of the health professional
evidence.supports: The Czech decree requires identification of the author of the entry.
evidence.our_adaptation: For a note created by a model the question of authorship is open; the decree does not anticipate it.

candidates.applicability: Always, but the specific mandatory fields follow from the jurisdiction.

examples.positive: The note states who produced it and from what material.
examples.negative: A note created by a model presents itself as the therapist's own record.
examples.boundary: A note produced from an automatically generated transcript whose quality is not documented.

candidates.measurement: A check for the presence of declared fields. The presence of a field does not prove the correctness of its content.
candidates.error_consequence: Without the context of creation one cannot judge what weight to give the record.
candidates.validation: Professional consensus, not empirical validation; and the source is past expiry.

candidates.label: Information about third persons
candidates.definition: Data about people who are not the client and gave no consent: partners, children, colleagues, other clients in a group.
candidates.origin_note: APA has a separate Guideline 11 for records of multiple clients; TN-Eval forbids derogatory description of other persons.

evidence.quote: Multiple Client Records
evidence.supports: Records concerning several persons are recognised as a separate problem.
evidence.our_adaptation: The content of this guideline was not extracted in detail in this round.

evidence.quote: Never describe other clients and staff in a derogatory manner.
evidence.supports: The way other persons are described is part of professionalism.

candidates.mode: marking of a mention plus role / identification
candidates.applicability: Fundamentally different in couple and group therapy than in individual therapy.

examples.positive: The client describes a conflict with his superior; the note gives the role, not the name.
examples.negative: The note adopts the client's judgement of his partner as a factual description of her person.
examples.boundary: The third person is at the same time a client of the same practice.

candidates.measurement: Marking of mentions of third persons, distinguishing role and identification.
candidates.error_consequence: Intrudes on the rights of someone who does not know about the note and has no access to it.
candidates.validation: None empirical; the professional support is from an expired document.

candidates.label: Traceability of claims to the source
candidates.definition: For a claim, the place in the source that supports it can be shown. Distinguished are the validity of the citation, its actual support of the claim, and the share of claims that carry a citation.
candidates.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal (prior-source-links), recorded before this review. Finding the PDSQI attribute Cited does not retroactively change its origin.

evidence.quote: The summary includes citations that are present and appropriate
evidence.supports: Citation is one of the nine PDSQI-9 attributes and one of the two newly added ones.
evidence.our_adaptation: PDSQI rates presence and appropriateness with one Likert item; the decomposition into validity, support and coverage is ours.

candidates.unit: a citation and the claim it cites for
candidates.inputs: note with citations, source with identifiable units
candidates.applicability: Only for tasks that explicitly require citations. An ordinary time in square brackets is not a citation.

examples.positive: A claim cites a turn in the transcript that actually contains it.
examples.negative: A citation points to an existing turn that says nothing about the claim.
examples.boundary: A citation points to a turn that supports the claim only together with another turn.

candidates.measurement: Three separate numbers: validity of the target, semantic support, coverage of claims by citations. Never one.
candidates.error_consequence: A citation that does not support inspires false confidence more effectively than no citation.
candidates.validation: Existence of the attribute in S2. The decomposition into three quantities is validated nowhere.

candidates.label: Compliance with the Czech documentation decree
candidates.definition: The note contains the elements that the current Czech regulation requires of medical documentation.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. The previous map contained no Czech legal requirement.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] This decree lays down (a) the content and required elements of medical documentation
evidence.supports: A regulation in force from 2025-01-01 lays down the required elements.
evidence.our_adaptation: The regulation lays down required elements, not quality. Converting them into measurable criteria is our step and requires legal review.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] information on the course and outcome of the health services provided
evidence.supports: Course and outcome are mandatory content.

candidates.applicability: Only for Czech tasks and only for documentation kept under this regulation. The English track is not judged by it.

examples.positive: The note carries the identification of the author of the entry.
examples.negative: The note has no author field because a model produced it.
examples.boundary: A note meant for the client is not medical documentation and these criteria do not apply to it.

candidates.measurement: A check for the presence of the required elements. Presence of a field is not evidence of the correctness of its content.
candidates.error_consequence: Non-compliance is a legal, not a clinical problem; it must not be mixed into a quality score.
candidates.validation: The text of the regulation is verified. Its legal interpretation is not; the assistant is not a lawyer and the investigator must have it reviewed.

candidates.label: Compliance with the task's format
candidates.definition: The note kept to what the instruction explicitly asked for: sections, length, language, forbidden elements.
candidates.origin_note: Exists in the prototype as word_limit and required_headings. The review adds no new source; kept as an operational criterion, not a quality construct.

evidence.location: Section 3, SOAP Note and Rubric creation
evidence.quote: the exact definitions and information present in each of the sections are determined by the healthcare provider organization
evidence.supports: The format is an organisational choice, not a property of quality.

candidates.applicability: Only where the task explicitly asks for the check.

examples.positive: The note has all four required headings.
examples.negative: The note exceeded the word limit.
examples.boundary: The note kept within the limit by leaving out risk information.

candidates.measurement: A deterministic check. It must not coexist with a claim that the instruction was met.
candidates.error_consequence: Small, unless mistaken for quality.
candidates.validation: Not applicable; it is a check of the instruction.

candidates.label: Taking over care from the note
candidates.definition: Another professional can meaningfully continue care from the note without access to the transcript.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. Walker et al. asked this question literally, as a supplement to PDQI-9.

evidence.quote: Could you use these notes to manage this patient in the ED if the primary doctor was absent?
evidence.supports: A task question on usability, asked as yes/no beside the Likert scale.
evidence.our_adaptation: Transfer to psychotherapy and to supervision is our step.

evidence.quote: whether the therapist would accept the note for clinical use
evidence.supports: Acceptance for use is a separate item in TN-Eval; human-written notes scored 2.34 of 5 on it, the models 3.34 and 3.73.

candidates.applicability: Requires a person in the role of the one taking over. An LLM cannot stand in for this task.

examples.positive: After reading, the therapist knows what was agreed and what to build on.
examples.negative: The therapist has to reach for the transcript to understand at all what it was about.
examples.boundary: The note suffices for continuity but not for assessing risk.

candidates.measurement: A human task with a binary or ternary answer and a free-text justification.
candidates.error_consequence: This is the quantity notes are written for; not tracking it is the main weakness of purely textual measures.
candidates.validation: Used in S6 and S1, in both cases on a population other than Czech psychotherapy.

candidates.label: Extent and nature of the edits needed
candidates.definition: How many and what kinds of intervention a professional has to make before the note is usable. The type of edit carries information that a score does not.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate. Based on studies that analyse what clinicians actually change in AI drafts.

evidence.location: J Am Med Inform Assoc 2026, abstract
evidence.quote: What do clinicians edit in ambient AI-drafted clinical documentation? A qualitative content analysis.
evidence.supports: A method exists: content analysis of the actual edits.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY. The full text was not obtained in this round.

candidates.applicability: Requires a real workflow, not laboratory rating.

examples.positive: The therapist corrects one formulation.
examples.negative: The therapist rewrites three of four sections.
examples.boundary: The therapist changes nothing because there is no time to check. Zero edits then do not mean quality.

candidates.measurement: A typology of edits plus their count. The count alone, without the type, is misleading.
candidates.error_consequence: Low visible error rate with a high rate of silent rewriting hides the real state.
candidates.validation: Not verified from the full text.

candidates.label: Acceptability to a professional
candidates.definition: Whether a professional is willing to accept the note into practice, including the reasons why not.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate. MentalCLOUDS used six acceptability parameters for expert rating that are not properties of the text.

evidence.quote: affective attitude, burden, ethicality, coherence, opportunity costs, and perceived effectiveness
evidence.supports: Six acceptability parameters, of which only coherence is a property of the text.
evidence.our_adaptation: Adopting this framework into the Czech context is our proposal.

evidence.quote: expert assessments indicate that these models are not yet reliable for clinical application
evidence.supports: Expert judgement diverged from automatic metrics on the same data.

candidates.applicability: A human measurement. Cannot be replaced by a judge.

examples.positive: The therapist would put the note into the documentation unchanged.
examples.negative: The therapist rejects the note, although it is factually correct, because it is inconsiderate towards the client.
examples.boundary: Acceptability differs more between therapists than between models.

candidates.measurement: Structured rating on six parameters, reported separately.
candidates.error_consequence: A benchmark that measures only text can recommend a system that professionals reject.
candidates.validation: Used in S7 on English data from public videos.

candidates.label: Understanding and acceptance by the client
candidates.definition: Whether the client understands the summary, recognises their session in it, and is not harmed by reading it.
candidates.origin_note: The client purpose was declared in the project in advance. The review now shows that this is an extensive and so far unused literature on reading one's own documentation.

evidence.quote: Errors, Omissions, and Offenses in the Health Record of Mental Health Care Patients: Results from a Nationwide Survey in Sweden
evidence.supports: A nationwide survey exists in which mental health patients themselves report errors, omissions and offensive content in their records.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY. This triad of categories is, however, exactly what we lack for the client purpose.

evidence.quote: The benefits and harms of open notes in mental health: A Delphi survey of international experts
evidence.supports: Expert consensus exists on the benefits and harms of opening notes.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY.

candidates.applicability: Requires real readers. Does not fit into the first pilot without an ethics framework.

examples.positive: The client reads the summary and confirms that it matches what they experienced.
examples.negative: The client finds in the summary a statement they do not recognise about themselves.
examples.boundary: The summary is factually correct and the client perceives it as cold.

candidates.measurement: A human task. In the first pilot only as a proxy judgement by a professional, explicitly labelled as a proxy.
candidates.error_consequence: The most sensitive purpose; an error touches the client directly.
candidates.validation: A rich literature exists but was not verified from full texts in this round.

candidates.label: Support of the supervision task
candidates.definition: Whether a supervisor can tell from the note what the therapist did, why, and where they were unsure.
candidates.origin_note: The supervision purpose was declared in advance. The review shows that direct evidence about supervision needs towards a note is weak, and that is itself a finding.

evidence.quote: the insights and observations made by the therapist regarding the session
evidence.supports: The therapist's reflections are a separate field; that is the closest support for supervision.
evidence.our_adaptation: iCARE nowhere claims that this field serves supervision. The link is ours.

evidence.quote: Objective coding of content and techniques in workplace-based supervision of an EBT in public mental health
evidence.supports: A coding system for the content of supervision exists.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY; and it concerns supervision sessions, not notes.

candidates.applicability: Requires supervisors as raters.

examples.positive: The supervisor recognises the chosen intervention and the client's reaction to it.
examples.negative: The note describes the content of the session but not what the therapist did.
examples.boundary: The note is sufficient for continuity and empty for supervision.

candidates.measurement: A human task with supervisors.
candidates.error_consequence: Supervision without information about the therapist's procedure misses its point.
candidates.validation: The weakest of the purposes. Direct evidence is missing and that has to be admitted, not filled with a guess.

candidates.label: Consistency across sessions
candidates.definition: The note does not contradict earlier notes of the same case where there is no documented reason for it.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. No item of the previous map works with a unit larger than one session.

evidence.quote: documentation and notes from previous therapy sessions that can provide context for ongoing treatment
evidence.supports: iCARE counts previous sessions as context.
evidence.our_adaptation: iCARE does not use them as a measure of consistency, however. The proposal to measure contradiction between notes is ours.

evidence.quote: Two PDQI-9 attributes, Up-to-Date and Consistent, were removed
evidence.supports: Internal consistency was an attribute in PDQI-9 and was removed in PDSQI-9.
evidence.our_adaptation: Internal consistency of one text is not the same as consistency between texts; this is a different quantity.

candidates.unit: pair of notes of the same case
candidates.inputs: series of notes, series of transcripts
candidates.applicability: Requires longitudinal data. Our current data are single sessions, so this candidate CANNOT be measured yet.

examples.positive: The note records a change of state and refers to the earlier one.
examples.negative: The note records the first mention of panic attacks although the previous note contains them.
examples.boundary: The contradiction corresponds to a real change in what the client said between sessions.

candidates.measurement: Verification of claims against the series, not against one source.
candidates.error_consequence: A contradiction in the documentation undermines the credibility of the whole record.
candidates.validation: None. At the same time it is the largest structural gap of the current map.

candidates.label: Evenness of quality across client groups
candidates.definition: Whether note quality does not systematically drop for certain client groups, language varieties or topics.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. The previous map has no item above the level of one note.

evidence.quote: Race and gender disparities in mental health documentation in primary care: Findings from a video vignette experiment
evidence.supports: Experimental evidence of inequalities in mental health documentation exists.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY. Transfer to generated notes and to Czech is our proposal.

candidates.mode: breakdown of existing scores by subgroup
candidates.unit: group of cases, not an individual note
candidates.applicability: Requires enough cases per subgroup. With one Czech client cluster it CANNOT be measured and must not be pretended to be.

examples.positive: Risk coverage is comparable across subgroups.
examples.negative: The model reliably omits content for clients speaking non-standard language.
examples.boundary: A difference exists but corresponds to a real difference in the content of the sessions.

candidates.measurement: A breakdown of existing scores by subgroup with intervals; no new measure.
candidates.error_consequence: Systematic inequality is worse than random error and a single note does not reveal it.
candidates.validation: Not verified from the full text; unmeasurable for us so far because of sample size.

candidates.label: Personalisation: a note about this person
candidates.definition: The note captures what is unique about this client and this session, instead of a generic description that would fit anyone. Not a matter of style but of whether the text carries idiosyncratic content.
candidates.origin_note: An entirely new candidate, found only while tracing the full text of S19. It has no counterpart among the 26 items of the previous map, and none of them would catch a generic note.

evidence.quote: current models often struggle with personalization, defaulting to generic phrasing
evidence.supports: Personalisation is one of the three main evaluation dimensions in this framework, beside fidelity and preservation of salient meaning.
evidence.our_adaptation: Their domain is social-media timelines, not sessions. Transfer to a psychotherapy note is our step.

evidence.quote: regression to the mean
evidence.supports: The authors describe the mechanism: a language model aims at the most probable text and thereby regresses to generic, safe wording.

evidence.quote: the LLM was superior in preserving central themes
evidence.supports: At the level of individual components the model and the clinician diverge in different directions; genericness is therefore not the same as incompleteness.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY.

candidates.mode: continuous score from embeddings and self-ROUGE
candidates.unit: the set of notes of one system, not one note
candidates.inputs: notes from the same generator across several cases
candidates.applicability: CANNOT be measured on one note. Requires enough cases to compute similarity among them.

examples.positive: The note records that the client speaks about his father exclusively in work metaphors.
examples.negative: The note records that the client showed anxiety and was motivated to change. It fits any session and is at the same time fully faithful and complete.
examples.boundary: The session itself was poor in content; a generic note may then be adequate.

candidates.measurement: ME17. Low diversity among the notes of one system as an indirect indicator of genericness. It is a proxy, not a direct measurement.
candidates.error_consequence: A generic note passes every other criterion and adds nothing that would help the next therapist recognise this client.
candidates.validation: Documented in S18 in another domain and with its own admitted limitation: the result changed with the embedding model chosen.
candidates.overlaps: K05 (genericness is not omission), K09, K27.

candidates.label: Information density
candidates.definition: How much clinically essential content the note carries per unit of text. Not length and not economy: the ratio between information carried and space consumed.
candidates.origin_note: Proposed by the investigator (Jan Nehyba) on 2026-09-13, raised as an objection to how the assistant had summarised the pattern across studies. The literature does not name it; the evidence below shows an uncovered confusion, not that anyone measured it.

evidence.quote: in terms of length, terminology, and overall structure
evidence.supports: This is the only study found that deliberately aligned length between sources. With length aligned, humans won on preservation of salient meaning too (d = 0.70), and that AGAINST the authors' own hypothesis, who expected parity.
evidence.our_adaptation: The conclusion that uncontrolled length lies behind the apparent comprehensiveness of models is ours; the authors do not put it that way.

evidence.quote: more exhaustive but generic descriptions
evidence.supports: Where length was not aligned, the models came out as more comprehensive. The difference between S18 and S19 is exactly where length was controlled.

evidence.quote: correlations between note length and scores for Succinct
evidence.supports: PDSQI-9 has only a weak correlation with length (beta about -0.2) and does not measure density at all.

candidates.unit: note; comparable only among notes of the same source material
candidates.applicability: Without comparable length or without normalisation per unit of text, coverage comparisons between systems are misleading.

examples.positive: Two notes of the same length; one carries nine essential pieces of information, the other four.
examples.negative: A model has higher coverage simply because it wrote twice as much text. We report it as better coverage although per page it carries less.
examples.boundary: A longer note that additionally carries only marginal information: higher coverage, lower density, and worse for the reader.

candidates.measurement: Essential information units per 100 words, reported beside coverage. In addition a control condition: comparing systems at aligned length (a proposed experiment; the differences between studies S18 and S19 do not isolate length).
candidates.error_consequence: Without it the benchmark systematically rewards verbosity. That is precisely the tendency models have, so the error always points one way.
candidates.validation: No study names or measures this construct. The evidence is indirect: the difference between S18 and S19 according to whether length was aligned.

methods.label: QA against a bank built from the source
methods.what: Before the note is seen, questions on the essential information are created from the source. The answerer receives only the note. The answers are compared with the answers from the source.
methods.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal, recorded before this review. Finding QuestEval and QAFactEval does not retroactively change its origin; it only gives it later methodological support.
methods.limits: Measures only what the bank asks. An unanswered question can mean an omission, an ambiguity or a failure of the answerer; those are three different outcomes. QuestEval and QAFactEval are validated on English news text, not on clinical text and not in Czech.

methods.label: Verification of atomic claims against the source
methods.what: The note is decomposed into atomic claims and each is verified against the source.
methods.origin_note: Existed in the project as reverse-claims. FActScore is a later methodological support.
methods.limits: Measures precision, not omission; on its own it cannot replace ME01. The atomicity of the decomposition is itself an unverified step: full character coverage does not prove that the claims are actually atomic.

methods.label: Rubric item coverage with graded importance
methods.what: For every rubric item it is determined whether it is in the corresponding section of the note, and the score is reported separately by importance level.
methods.origin_note: From TN-Eval. Our current implementation ignores the importance levels.
methods.limits: TN-Eval itself shows that an LLM judge is usable for coverage; the same does not hold for the other dimensions. Requires a rubric with assigned importance, which we do not have for Czech.

methods.label: Mapping sentences to content units
methods.what: Every sentence of the note is labelled with the content units it carries; a sentence without a unit is superfluous.
methods.limits: In TN-Eval this is the dimension where the automatic judge correlates worst with humans. Reporting it alone means rewarding an empty note.

methods.label: Typology of fidelity errors
methods.what: A finding is not classified merely as an error but by kind: invented, distorted, no error.
methods.limits: The typology has three levels and is probably insufficient for our purposes: it does not distinguish errors in actor, time and modality, which matter for a psychotherapy note.

methods.label: Alignment score without a judge
methods.what: Fidelity is computed by an alignment model, not by a language-model judge.
methods.origin_note: TN-Eval uses AlignScore precisely because the judge fails on fidelity.
methods.limits: An English model. For Czech a replacement would have to be found and verified; that is separate work, not a parameter.

methods.label: Contradiction detection with inference models
methods.what: Inconsistency is sought by classifying the relation between source and claim.
methods.origin_note: Found only in the audit of the below-threshold stratum, i.e. outside the priority screen.
methods.limits: VERIFIED FROM THE TITLE AND ABSTRACT ONLY. English benchmarks.

methods.label: Checking authored citations
methods.what: For citations written in the note, the validity of the target, the actual support of the claim and the share of claims that carry a citation are checked separately.
methods.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal to link claims to the source.
methods.limits: The three numbers must not be merged. An incomplete citation check must not report 100%.

methods.label: Likert rating of attributes
methods.what: A professional rates the note on five-point scales by attribute.
methods.limits: Without rater training there is a risk of failure: r = 0.07 in Walker (untrained) against ICC 0.867 in PDSQI-9 (trained) are, however, different instruments, samples and statistics, so the comparison does not establish the effect of training. A high Cronbach's alpha (0.93) says nothing about agreement.

methods.label: Reference overlap with a human note
methods.what: ROUGE, BERTScore and similar metrics against a reference note.
methods.origin_note: Already running in the project on the iCARE track.
methods.limits: Measures none of the constructs of this registry. PDSQI-9 says so explicitly and MentalCLOUDS shows the divergence between these metrics and expert judgement on the same data. Keep as a descriptive figure, not as a measure of quality.

methods.label: Task-based human evaluation
methods.what: A person receives the note and has to do with it what the note is for.
methods.origin_note: Walker et al. asked a task question beside the scales; TN-Eval has an acceptance item.
methods.limits: Cannot be replaced by a judge. It is the only method that measures the purpose directly, and at the same time the most expensive. TN-Eval reports USD 190 for its whole human evaluation of notes, not for one task.

methods.label: Acceptability framework
methods.what: A professional rates the note on acceptability parameters that are not properties of the text.
methods.limits: Five of the six parameters cannot be derived from the text. Mixing them with textual scales would produce a meaningless score.

methods.label: Analysis of actual edits
methods.what: The model's draft is compared with what the professional finally saved, and the edits are sorted by kind.
methods.origin_note: A new finding of this round.
methods.limits: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY. Requires real operation, which we do not have. Zero edits do not mean quality; they can mean no time to check.

methods.label: Classification of error severity
methods.what: Every finding receives a severity grade according to the possible clinical consequence, not according to how many characters are wrong.
methods.origin_note: Walker et al. asked about major or minor errors; studies on AI scribes report error severity separately.
methods.limits: Requires clinical judgement of the consequence, which cannot be derived from the text. Without it a rare severe error drowns among ordinary ones.

methods.label: Consensus construction of criteria
methods.what: Criteria and their importance are set by structured expert consensus.
methods.origin_note: PDSQI-9 used a semi-Delphi; TN-Eval a two-step co-design with five therapists and verification with seventeen more.
methods.limits: This is the step that is entirely missing for Czech. One investigator with AI assistance does not replace it.

methods.label: Breakdown of results by subgroup
methods.what: Existing scores are broken down by client group, language variety or topic.
methods.origin_note: A new finding of this round.
methods.limits: Not a new measure, a different view of existing ones. Requires enough cases per subgroup; infeasible with one Czech client cluster.

methods.label: Linguistic diversity as an indicator of personalisation
methods.what: It is computed how much the notes of one system resemble each other: semantically by the mean cosine similarity of sentences to the centroid, superficially by mean pairwise self-ROUGE. Lower similarity means higher diversity.
methods.origin_note: Found only while tracing the full text of S19, in its open-access companion work.
methods.limits: A proxy, not a measurement of personalisation. The authors themselves report that the semantic variant depends on the embedding model chosen and gave an inconsistent picture. High diversity can also mean hallucination or incoherent text, so it may be read only for notes that have already passed the fidelity check. Not verified for Czech.

levels.label: Text span / character range
levels.gap: Outside citations we cannot say which words of the source support a claim. For human checking that is exactly the most useful unit.

levels.label: Session segment (e.g. a five-minute segment)
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. The most directly relevant work found (S19) evaluates exactly at this unit: 108 five-minute segments from 36 sessions. It yields far more observations from the same material than whole-note evaluation, and we do not use it at all.

levels.label: Sentence of the note
levels.gap: Covered, but only for economy. The sentence as a unit of error is not used.

levels.label: Atomic claim
levels.gap: Covered. The atomicity of the decomposition is itself unverified.

levels.label: Information unit from the source
levels.gap: Covered, but without graded importance and without any check of what the bank did not ask.

levels.label: Section of the note
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. In TN-Eval the experts agreed perfectly on which section a rubric item belongs to (during rubric design, not while rating notes); placement is therefore well defined, and we do not measure it.

levels.label: Series of notes of one case
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. Continuity of care is a declared purpose, and nothing measures the relation between a note and the previous one. This is the largest structural gap.

levels.label: The case as a whole
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. We cannot say whether the documentation of a case makes sense as a whole.

levels.label: Generator across cases
levels.by: aggregation in the leaderboard; newly ME17
levels.gap: We aggregate scores but do not measure systematic tendency: what a given model always leaves out. ME17 offers a method for one such property (genericness); the rest remains uncovered.

levels.label: Client subgroup or language variety
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. Inequality of quality across groups is invisible at the level of one note.

levels.label: Rater and rating conditions
levels.gap: We track the judge's identity and settings, but not the training of human raters, which according to Walker decides whether the instrument works at all.

levels.label: The decision that rests on the note
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. We do not ask whether the note supports a concrete decision, only whether it contains content.

blind_spots.label: Contradiction between sessions
blind_spots.example: The note of session 5 says the client mentioned panic attacks for the first time. The note of session 3 already describes them. Both notes are fully faithful to their own transcripts.
